name: AI Agent Security
blurb: Agent kill chains, cascading multi-agent failure, circuit breakers, agent-to-agent trust boundaries, and runtime supervision of autonomous systems.

items.name: Agentic threat taxonomy
items.note: OWASP's agentic threat model covers cascading failure, excessive agency, and inter-agent trust - the map for securing systems that act.

items.name: MCP security best practices
items.note: The protocol's own security guidance: confused-deputy risks, token passthrough, consent, and tool trust in agent toolchains.

domains.body: Agent security is envelope design: machine-enforced limits on what an agent can spend, touch, and trigger, circuit breakers that halt execution when behavior exits the envelope, and trust boundaries between agents so that one compromised or confused agent cannot instruct another into escalation. Humans are too slow to supervise machine-speed loops in real time, so the envelope has to be enforced by machinery, with the protocol-level guidance for tool ecosystems, including MCP's security best practices, defining where those boundaries sit.
domains.label: Architecture and Engineering

domains.body: Cascading failure is the agent-native incident class: every individual agent behaved within its rules and the system still failed, because interactions compounded in ways no single rule anticipated. Runtime supervision watches the system, not just the agents, with kill-switch protocols that are pre-authorized and rehearsed rather than improvised mid-incident, and post-incident rebuilds that ask what the agent learned, what it changed, and what those changes caused downstream.
domains.label: Security Operations

domains.body: Tool design is where agent security is won or lost in products: narrowly scoped tools with validated arguments, destructive operations gated behind confirmation, side-effecting calls logged with full context, and tool descriptions treated as an injection surface because agents read them as instructions. A well-designed tool set makes the worst reachable action survivable; a broad one makes every prompt injection a potential incident.
domains.label: Application and Product Security

domains.body: Autonomy is earned, not configured: governance defines the tiers of action an agent may take alone, with human review, or not at all, and expands an agent's tier only on evidence from adversarial evaluation and operating history. A supervision model that grants full autonomy on day one is not a policy, it is the absence of one recorded in writing.
domains.label: Security Governance and Risk Management

domains.body: Third-party agents and the MCP servers they connect through are a new vendor class arriving faster than assessment categories can form, and this site tracks the registry ecosystem at the scale of nearly two thousand servers. Assessing them means asking about tool provenance, what hidden context and instructions ship with the integration, and how authority attenuates when your agent delegates to a vendor's agent across an organizational boundary.
